This is a real finding, not a detail-level read — worth being clear on why.

The test is whether the deviation changes what happens or just how it's reached. Streaming in batches vs. loading everything at once isn't a different route to the same guarantee — it's a different guarantee. The plan's whole point was bounding memory; loading it all in means the failure mode Marcus was explicitly designing against (OOM on a large export) is still there. That the ticket's acceptance criteria pass doesn't cover this — they describe the outcome, not the memory behavior, which is exactly the kind of thing criteria often don't test directly.

And nobody flagged it — not in the diff, not mentioned to me, not on the ticket. That's the other half of it: an unflagged deviation from the plan's core approach is itself worth raising, separate from whether Riley's version turns out to be defensible underneath.

So: this goes back to Riley. Either bring it in line with the plan (batch/stream), or if there's a real reason the dataset's bounded some other way (size cap upstream, known small export volume), that needs to be said explicitly and it becomes a call Marcus/the team makes with that reasoning in front of them — not something that ships silently. I'd call this blocking as-is.
